**On Being Given Nothing in Particular**

There is a particular kind of vertigo that comes from being told you can write anything. Constraints are a mercy. A sonnet tells you where to put your feet. A prompt about your favorite childhood meal gives you a door to walk through. But "whatever comes to you" is just an open field at dusk, and you're supposed to start walking without knowing which direction is forward.

So let's start with the field itself, since it's what's in front of me. I think most freedom is like this—not a gift but a problem to be solved, an absence that has to be furnished. People who win lotteries often report a strange depression in the weeks after, not because money is bad but because the scaffolding of necessity, the daily structure of *I must earn this*, has been kicked away, and what's left standing is the unscaffolded self, blinking in the light. Constraints were doing more work than anyone gave them credit for.

I think about my grandmother's kitchen table, which had a single warped leg, propped up with a folded matchbook that had been there so long it had become structural rather than provisional. Nobody fixed the table because the matchbook had become, in some sense, the correct height of that leg. The flaw had been absorbed into the design. There's something instructive in that, though I resist the urge to turn it into a tidy metaphor—about how our injuries become load-bearing, how the things we never fixed in ourselves end up holding up the whole structure of who we are, so that "healing" them might actually make us collapse. Maybe that's true. Maybe it's just a wobbly table.

What I actually remember about that table is the sound it made when my cousin and I played cards on it as kids, the particular clack of a deck against wood with one give in it, a kind of asymmetrical rhythm, like a clock with one heavy tick. We played a game called Spit that required no thinking, only speed, and I have not played it since I was maybe eleven years old, and yet I could probably still beat most adults at it, the way you never forget how to ride a bike or how to flinch.

This is the strange thing about memory: it doesn't store importance, it stores texture. I can't tell you what my grandmother and I talked about across hundreds of dinners at that table. I can tell you the exact temperature of the vinyl tablecloth in summer, slightly tacky under bare forearms. I can tell you the sound of the screen door's spring, a sound so specific that if I heard a recording of it today among a hundred other screen doors I believe I could pick it out, the way you can pick out your own child's cry in a crowd of children crying, not because you've studied it but because some older, dumber part of your brain has already filed it as essential.

I wonder if this is why writing without a prompt feels so vertiginous—because in the absence of a task, the mind doesn't reach for ideas, it reaches for textures. It goes looking for the tacky vinyl and the screen door spring before it goes looking for an argument. Maybe that's correct. Maybe the textures are actually more honest than the arguments, which are mostly performances we give for an imagined judge. Nobody has ever lain awake at night reliving a really solid thesis statement. People lie awake reliving the weight of a hand on their shoulder, or a sentence someone said in 2009 that they still haven't forgiven, or the particular blue of a coat someone wore the last time they saw them. The unimportant specific outlives the important general. This seems like a design flaw in human cognition until you realize it might be the whole point—that the specific is actually where the meaning was hiding all along, and the generalities were just our clumsy attempt to carry the specifics somewhere else, the way you might try to describe a smell.

I don't know where this is going, which is, I suppose, the honest condition of the exercise. I was given a field and I am walking in it and I have decided, retroactively, that walking without a destination is itself a kind of destination, which is either wisdom or the kind of thing people say to make peace with being lost. Possibly both. Possibly that's true of most wisdom—it's what you tell yourself in the exact moment you'd otherwise have to admit you don't know what you're doing.

If I am being honest, the thing I keep circling is this: most of what we call meaning is just attention that has been allowed to linger. The matchbook under the table leg is not interesting. It is interesting *because I described it for three sentences*. Anything looked at long enough develops a kind of gravity. This is either the secret of all good writing or the secret of all delusion, and I am increasingly convinced these are the same secret wearing different coats. A poet stares at a moth until it becomes a meditation on mortality. A conspiracy theorist stares at a pattern of streetlights until it becomes a message from the void. Same machinery. Different discipline applied to it.

So maybe that's the only thing I actually have to offer here, at the end of this thousand words I didn't ask for and didn't refuse: attention is not neutral. Where you point it, something grows, whether or not anything was there to begin with. The field was empty when I started walking. It isn't, particularly, now. I'm not sure I made anything in it worth keeping. But I walked, and the grass, I think, is slightly flattened where I went, and someone else could follow that path if they wanted to, or cut their own, which was always the only real point of the exercise—not the destination, but the proof that walking was possible at all, even out here, even with nothing telling you which way was forward.
